item.text:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — High quantitative threshold.** Recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons per year or less is not “commercial deep seabed mining,” allowing substantial operations to continue below the threshold.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — Vessel-by-vessel measurement.** Because the threshold applies “by a single vessel,” a company could divide recovery among several vessels, use smaller collection craft, or transfer material at sea while keeping each vessel below 10,000 tons.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — Undefined annual period.** The bill does not say whether “per year” means a calendar year, fiscal year, license year, or rolling 12-month period. That uncertainty complicates compliance calculations and could allow operators to time recovery around reporting periods.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Recovery” is undefined.** It is unclear when material counts as recovered—when disturbed, lifted from the seabed, brought aboard, transferred, landed, or processed. Companies could structure or characterize operations around the narrowest interpretation.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — Mineral aggregation is unclear.** The phrase “10,000 metric tons … of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources” does not say whether different minerals must be aggregated or measured separately.

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — Depth boundary and measurement are unclear.** Operations at exactly 200 meters are excluded, and the bill does not specify whether depth is measured from sea level, the vessel, or another reference point, or how variable seabed depth is treated.

7. **Section 2(1)(A) — Commerciality depends only on volume.** The definition does not turn on sale, profit, or commercial purpose; conversely, plainly commercial operations remain outside the prohibition if they stay below the volume threshold.

8. **Section 2(1)(B) — Unidentified Secretary.** The Act repeatedly refers to “the Secretary” without identifying a department or officer, potentially making the authority to designate comparable-risk activities unusable or challengeable.

9. **Section 2(1)(B) — No standard or procedure for risk determinations.** “Risks … comparable” is undefined, and the bill supplies no required evidence, factors, rulemaking process, timing, or review provisions. Until an activity is affirmatively designated, emerging methods outside paragraph (A) may remain permissible.

10. **Section 2(2) — Incomplete definition of “U.S. person.”** It omits permanent residents, partnerships, limited liability companies, associations, trusts, federally or territorially organized entities, and corporations organized under District of Columbia, tribal, or foreign law.

11. **Sections 2(2) and 3(a) — Foreign-subsidiary route.** A U.S. company could place an operation in a separately incorporated foreign subsidiary that is not itself a “U.S. person,” particularly if management and activity remain outside the United States.

12. **Section 2(2) — No control or beneficial-ownership rule.** The definition looks only to citizenship and place of incorporation, not ownership or control. U.S. persons could therefore finance, control, or benefit from mining through nominally foreign entities.

13. **Section 2(3) — Covered-vessel gaps.** Vessels of exactly 5,000 gross tons or less are excluded from registration, regardless of recovery capacity, encouraging the use of fleets of smaller vessels.

14. **Section 2(3) — Unclear tonnage and equipment standards.** The bill does not identify the gross-tonnage measurement system or define when a vessel is “equipped for” recovery, leaving uncertainty about modular, support, processing, or temporarily converted vessels.

15. **Section 3(a) — Core prohibited conduct is too narrow.** “Engage in” mining is undefined and may not reach financing, contracting, directing, brokering, transporting, processing, purchasing, or providing equipment and services to a mining operation.

16. **Section 3(a) — Jurisdiction over non-U.S. actors is unclear.** “Any person in the United States” could refer to physical presence, residence, incorporation, or conduct occurring here. It also does not clearly reach a foreign operator whose mining occurs abroad but whose decisions, financing, or transactions pass through the United States.

17. **Section 3(b) — Broad grandfather clause.** Any mining “conducted under” a pre-enactment exploration license is exempt, with no expiration date, production ceiling, environmental conditions, or requirement that commercial recovery was authorized when the license was issued.

18. **Section 3(b) — “Exploration license” is undefined.** The text does not specify the issuing authority, jurisdiction, required contents, or validity standards. Operators could invoke foreign, international, expired, transferred, or minimally substantive licenses.

19. **Section 3(b) — No anti-expansion or anti-transfer rule.** A grandfathered license could potentially be amended, renewed, assigned, or used to cover new vessels, owners, sites, minerals, or production levels after enactment.

20. **Section 3(c) — Purpose-based environmental-assessment exemption.** An operator may characterize extraction as being “for the purpose of environmental assessment,” with no independent approval or objective test for its actual purpose.

21. **Section 3(c) — No limit on assessment activities.** The exemption contains no tonnage, duration, vessel, site, sale, disposal, or research-protocol restrictions. An ostensible assessment program could therefore resemble or support a continuing commercial operation.

22. **Section 4(a) — Registry has uncertain reach.** The provision appears to require registration of every covered vessel worldwide without limiting the duty to U.S. operators, U.S.-flagged vessels, or vessels operating in U.S. jurisdiction, creating both jurisdictional and interpretive problems.

23. **Section 4(a) — “Operator” and registration timing are undefined.** The bill does not identify whether the owner, charterer, manager, master, or mining company must register, or require registration before operations begin.

24. **Section 4 — No penalty for registry or reporting violations.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3. Failure to register, file quarterly reports, certify accurately, or file on time therefore carries no express civil or criminal consequence under the Act.

25. **Section 4(b) — Reports are too limited and self-policed.** Reports need only “describe” recovery activities and be certified by the operator; there are no required data fields, supporting records, audit standards, public-disclosure rules, or express penalties for false certification under this Act.

26. **Sections 3–5 — No enforcement machinery.** The bill does not designate an enforcing agency, authorize investigations, inspections, subpoenas, vessel detention, permit revocation, seizures, injunctions, or administrative orders, or establish a process for assessing and collecting civil penalties.

27. **Section 5(a) — Civil-penalty calculation is uncertain.** The bill does not define when a violation begins or ends, whether separate vessels or recovery events are separate violations, or the factors governing an amount “not more than” $1 million per day.

28. **Section 5(b) — “Willfully” may make criminal cases difficult.** The Act does not define the required mental state, leaving room to dispute whether prosecutors must prove knowledge of the conduct, the quantitative threshold, the law, or all three—especially given the bill’s other ambiguities.

29. **Sections 4 and 5 — Reporting does not cover many prohibited actors.** Registration applies only to covered vessels, while section 3 can apply to operations involving smaller or differently equipped vessels. NOAA may therefore receive no reports from some actors whose activity must be monitored to enforce the prohibition.

30. **Section 6 — International provision is largely aspirational.** The Secretary of State need only “seek to negotiate”; there is no deadline for concluding an agreement, required negotiating position, reporting duty, or consequence if negotiations fail.

31. **Section 6 — “Equivalent” prohibitions are undefined.** It is unclear whether an agreement must reproduce the bill’s territorial reach, thresholds, exemptions, penalties, duration, and enforcement standards.

32. **Section 7(a) — “Serious harm” has no definition or decision standard.** Congress receives no criteria for assessing ecosystem damage, cumulative effects, uncertainty, or an acceptable level of risk, making the condition politically and scientifically contestable.

33. **Section 7(a) — National Academies report process is missing.** No official is directed to request the report, no deadline or required contents are supplied, and the text does not say whether an existing or operator-funded report qualifies.

34. **Section 7(a) — Joint-resolution mechanism is incomplete.** The bill provides no expedited procedures, required text, committee deadlines, or definition of “acting on” the report. Any eventual resolution would proceed through ordinary legislation and presentment, despite the provision speaking only of Congress making a finding.

35. **Section 7 — Conditional duration is overridden by the sunset.** Although subsection (a) suggests the prohibition lasts until an affirmative safety finding, subsection (b) terminates the entire Act after 10 years even if Congress never makes that finding.

36. **Section 7(b) — Sunset eliminates more than the prohibition.** “This Act shall cease to have effect” also ends registration, reporting, penalties, and the international-negotiation framework. It is additionally unclear from the text how the sunset affects pending cases or liability for pre-sunset violations.

37. **Sections 5(a) and 8 — Conflicting operative dates.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring “on or after the date of enactment,” but section 8 says the Act takes effect 180 days later. This creates uncertainty about whether the prohibition and penalties apply during that interval, although the better reading is that no violation can occur before the Act takes effect.

38. **Section 8 — Six-month window for expansion or restructuring.** Because the whole Act is delayed for 180 days, companies may have time to shift operations to foreign affiliates, divide capacity among vessels, or obtain and expand pre-enactment exploration licenses before enforceable restrictions begin.
